n: In this lesson we study sudden death from cardiovascular diseases. Sudden death occurs quickly and unexpectedly for those around, from an acute or latent chronic disease. To exclude violence, the corpse is opened. Cardiovascular diseases make up the main part of sudden death in adults. Microscopic, that is histopathological, examination is often the method that determines the cause of death, since macroscopic changes may be few or absent altogether. Aim of the lesson: to study histopathological methods and morphological signs.

First let us distinguish the terms. Formerly non-violent death was distinguished in two forms: unexpected and sudden. In unexpected death the disease was not previously detected, death occurs within 24 hours, in English unexpected death. In sudden death the disease was detected, and death occurs in a situation without danger, in English sudden death. This distinction is conventional: the person's attitude and the quality of medical care play a significant part. Remember: in the old division unexpected and sudden were not the same, whereas now most researchers take them as synonyms.

t: Five signs characteristic of unexpected death
n: We consider the five signs characteristic of unexpected death. First sign: the cause of death is always a disease. Often before death no symptoms are seen at all, or they are not clearly marked. Second and third signs: death occurs quickly, in a short time, and before it the state of health is completely or relatively good. Fourth sign: the circumstances of death always raise suspicion of violent death. Fifth sign: on examination of the corpse a vital disease that caused death is found.

t: Tasks of the expert and pathogenesis of sudden death
n: The expert has three tasks. To exclude violent death, to find and describe the pathological changes that caused death, and to determine the variant of thanatogenesis. Detecting acute infectious diseases and taking sanitary-epidemiological measures is also a task of the expert. As for pathogenesis, in death from a cardiac cause, ventricular fibrillation most often develops against a background of cardiosclerosis and myocardial damage. The conduction system is very resistant to ischaemia, so in early ischaemia its structural damage is not found. In death from a cerebral cause, cerebral oedema and swelling damage the neurons of the brainstem and stop breathing and circulation.

t: General morphological signs of sudden death
n: General morphological signs of sudden death: liquid blood in the heart and vessels, general venous congestion, small haemorrhages in the mucous-serous membranes and in the stroma of organs. The same signs are seen in asphyxia, since the pathogenesis of asphyxia and sudden death is similar. In chronic severe disease, hypertrophy and delipoidisation of the adrenal cortex are commoner; this is a stress reaction. Acute ischaemic damage of cortical neurons without glial reaction, and swelling of neurons in the subcortical nuclei, testify to the speed of death.

In adults, in the great majority of cases of unexpected death, that is 85–90 per cent, the cause is cardiovascular disease. Among the diseases of this system, atherosclerosis and hypertensive disease occupy the leading place. In bringing about unexpected death, atherosclerosis of the vessels of the heart and brain is of chief importance. Attention, there is a risk of error: 85–90 per cent relates only to adults. In children about 90 per cent of unexpected death is caused by acute respiratory diseases.

Atherosclerosis of the cardiac vessels appears as ischaemic heart disease. In this disease acute coronary insufficiency and myocardial infarction may cause unexpected death. For infarction to develop, at least 12–24 hours are needed after the coronary circulation is disturbed. Unexpected death usually occurs faster. Remember: acute coronary insufficiency and myocardial infarction are not the same. For infarction, the circulation must be disturbed for longer.

t: Simpson: coronary atherosclerosis and its complications
n: We consider coronary atherosclerosis and its complications after Simpson. Narrowing of a coronary artery by atheroma, that is stenosis, leads to chronic ischaemia of the myocardium, and ischaemic myocardium is electrically unstable. When the heart rate quickens, for example in exertion, a large meal or stress, the demand for oxygen rises. Ischaemia does not always reach infarction, but also reaches a fatal arrhythmia. Complications of a plaque: haemorrhage under the intima, rupture, downstream displacement of cholesterol fragments giving small infarcts, and thrombus formation. Coronary thrombosis lies at the basis of many complications of death, but at autopsy it is found variously, from 13 to 98 per cent.

In the mechanism of acute coronary insufficiency the main role is played by spasm of the coronary vessels. The importance of atherosclerosis is secondary. Here the atherosclerotic changes in the coronary vessels are not severe and marked. The chain is as follows: spasm of the coronary vessels leads to ischaemia of cardiomyocytes, an arrhythmogenic substance is released, then the spasm passes and blood flow is restored. As a result ventricular fibrillation occurs. Ventricular fibrillation is regarded as the immediate cause of death.

t: Sudden cardiac death: definition and the ischaemic stage of infarction
n: Sudden cardiac death occurs outside hospital, within 24 hours of an acute symptom. In expert examination it is taken as cardiac arrest with fibrillation. Macroscopic signs in the ischaemic stage of infarction: flaccidity of the myocardium and dilatation of the cavities. Microscopic sign: contracture in cardiomyocytes, that is segments of repeated contraction. Also found are fragmentation of cardiomyocytes, spasm of arteries, sludge in venules, filling of capillaries with plasma, small haemorrhages and interstitial oedema. A histochemical decrease in the activity of oxidative enzymes in cardiomyocytes helps to detect ischaemia, and the Rego stain is a convenient alternative.

Time is needed for the development of myocardial infarction. If circulation in the coronary vessels is disturbed for longer, infarction develops. The atherosclerotic changes are marked, and a thrombus may also be found in the vessel. For a clear infarct to form, the disturbance of the coronary circulation must last at least 12–24 hours. Unexpected death usually occurs faster, in a short time, and for that reason a clearly visible infarct is not seen. Attention, there is a risk of error: in acute coronary insufficiency spasm of the coronary vessels holds the main place, and it is not myocardial infarction.

The appearance and colour of the infarct focus change with time. After a few hours the focus is indistinct, flaccid and unevenly congested. So if death occurs after a few hours, the focus of necrosis cannot be clearly distinguished. In the second half of day 1, a clay-coloured focus and a rim of haemorrhage are seen. The focus itself is slightly raised because of oedema. Later a yellowish-grey or yellowish-green colour appears. The yellowish-grey colour is characteristic of the classical picture of infarction.

t: Infarct: stages of necrosis and organisation
n: In the stage of necrosis, a grey-yellow structureless area is seen in the myocardium with a haemorrhagic rim around it. Cardiomyocytes look uniformly hypereosinophilic, karyolysis is seen, and at the edge a leukocyte rampart forms over time. In organisation, granulation tissue and a scar form. In this stage too, sudden death from fibrillation is possible. Remember: thrombosis of the coronary artery is not decisive in diagnosing sudden cardiac death; it often develops secondarily against a background of infarction.

t: Immediate causes of death in myocardial infarction
n: In myocardial infarction, cardiogenic shock or asystole, that is cardiac arrest, may directly lead to death. Aneurysm of the heart and rupture of the heart wall may also be the immediate cause of death. In addition, thromboembolic complications may develop in the systemic circulation. So, complications of infarction leading to death: cardiogenic shock, asystole, cardiac aneurysm, rupture of the heart wall and thromboembolic complications.

t: Simpson: infarct complications and heart weight
n: Infarct complications and heart weight after Simpson. The infarct zone is weakest between day 3 and week 1 from clinical onset. If it ruptures, sudden death occurs from haemopericardium and cardiac tamponade. Rupture may be through the interventricular septum, that is a left-to-right shunt, or through a papillary muscle, that is mitral valve prolapse. The infarct heals by scar, that is fibrosis. A cardiac aneurysm may form, calcify and rupture. The average male heart is about 400 g; a heart heavier than 500 g is regarded as unstable. In aortic stenosis the heart may exceed 700 g.

t: Chronic ischaemic disease and coronary atherosclerosis
n: Chronic ischaemic disease appears as diffuse and small-focal cardiosclerosis and leads to electrical instability of the myocardium. Coronary atherosclerosis is characterised by the formation of plaques in the intima and narrowing of the lumen by 75 per cent or more. There may be signs of thrombosis or spasm: tearing of the intima, disruption of the elastic membrane, plasmatic imbibition and haemorrhage into the plaque. Sudden cardiac death in young persons with minimally altered coronary arteries may be the result of metabolic and microcirculatory disturbances.

In adults, in 85–90% of cases of unexpected death, the cause is cardiovascular disease. Among them atherosclerosis and hypertensive disease lead. Hypertensive disease is often seen together with ischaemic heart disease and cerebrovascular disease. It leads to unexpected death through acute heart failure, myocardial infarction or disturbance of cerebral circulation.

t: Histology of hypertension and alcoholic cardiomyopathy
n: We look at the histology of hypertension and alcoholic cardiomyopathy. In hypertension, at an early stage, hyperelastosis and hypertrophy of the muscle layer are found in muscular-type arteries. Left ventricular hypertrophy, hypertrophy of cardiomyocytes and diffuse cardiosclerosis are seen, and in the kidney some glomeruli are in a state of hyalinosis and sclerosis. In alcoholic cardiomyopathy, uneven hypertrophy of cardiomyocytes, lipofuscinosis, stromal lipomatosis, and diffuse and small-focal cardiosclerosis are found. To detect uneven hypertrophy, morphometry is used: the thickness of cardiomyocytes is measured with an ocular micrometer and the dispersion is calculated.

There are other cardiovascular diseases too. Myocarditis, rheumatism and heart defects may lead to unexpected death. Aneurysms and thrombophlebitis of various origins may also be a cause of unexpected death. In older children, endocarditis, myocarditis, and congenital and acquired heart defects may lead to unexpected death. That is, the causes are divided into groups in adults, in vessels and in older children.

Cardiomyopathies and channelopathies after Simpson. Primary diseases of the myocardium are characteristic of a younger group: in myocarditis and cardiomyopathies the structure is altered, whereas in channelopathies there is no morphological change. Myocarditis may be macroscopically "mottled", that is with pale or bloody foci. Histological confirmation requires many samples. HCM, that is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, is an inherited disease of sarcomere proteins, with myocyte disarray. DCM, that is dilated cardiomyopathy, is primary or from alcohol. ARVCM, that is arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, is with thinning of the right ventricle and fibro-fatty replacement. In channelopathies there is no change either to the eye or under the microscope, the defect is at the molecular level, in the Na, K and Ca channels. The importance of molecular testing is growing.

In constrictive, dilated and hypertrophic cardiomyopathies it is important to find foci of acute myocardial damage and signs of fibrillation. In idiopathic endocardial fibrosis and Lev's disease, the conduction system is examined histologically, and marked fibrosis and signs of fibrillation give the diagnosis. In myocarditis the macroscopic change may be only flaccidity, so the diagnosis is based only on histological examination. If bacterial endocarditis is complicated by thromboembolic syndrome, vital organs are damaged and this leads to sudden death.

Aortic aneurysms after Simpson. Among the arteries, apart from the heart, the commonest change in sudden death is an aneurysm. An atheromatous aneurysm in the elderly is in the abdominal aorta: the elastic part under the atheroma is damaged, the aneurysm is saccular or fusiform, the wall is calcified, and inside there is an old thrombus. A dissecting aneurysm begins in the thoracic aorta, with an intimal defect and weakness of the media. If it ruptures, blood is shed into the chest, abdomen or pericardium. It occurs mainly in hypertension, and in the young in Marfan syndrome. A syphilitic aneurysm is in the arch of the thoracic aorta, thin-walled, and is now rare.

As a complication of hypertension, medionecrosis of the aorta forms a dissecting aneurysm and may lead to sudden death. In histology, foci of breakdown filled with mucoid substance in the aortic media, that is Erdheim cysts, defects of elasticity, rupture and haemorrhage into the wall are seen. When an atherosclerotic aortic aneurysm ruptures, sclerosis, atrophy and foci of degeneration of the media, and acute haemorrhage, are found. A connective tissue capsule with siderophages and haemolysed blood show that a long time has passed since the rupture. A fresh rupture should be sought in the area of the plaque.

In thromboembolism of the pulmonary artery system, especially when large branches are involved, the source and age of the embolism must be established. The source is usually the right auricle, in atrial fibrillation. Or thrombosis of the deep veins of the legs and of the small pelvis, in hypodynamia and circulatory failure. To determine the age of the process, the reaction of the elements of the vessel wall to the embolus is assessed.

t: Microscopic examination: its place in the source and limitations
n: In unexpected death of children, the corpse, besides internal and external examination, undergoes histological, virological and bacteriological examinations. In unexpected death from respiratory infection, a specific microscopic change is found only in pneumocystis pneumonia and cytomegalovirus infection. In sudden infant death syndrome, SIDS for short, foci of emphysema and atelectasis occasionally occur in the lungs. Other laboratory examinations are usually negative. This shows the place of microscopic examination in the source and its limitations.

Attention, distinguish: spasm and infarction are not the same thing. In acute coronary insufficiency spasm of the coronary vessels holds the main place, and the importance of atherosclerosis is secondary. For infarction to develop, at least 12–24 hours are needed after the coronary circulation is disturbed, so in unexpected death a clear infarct is not seen. If death occurs after a few hours, the focus of necrosis is not clearly defined, and the myocardium is flaccid and unevenly congested. From other systems, unexpected death is seen less often: pneumonia, bronchial asthma, epilepsy, diabetes mellitus, gastric ulcer, Mallory–Weiss syndrome.

t: Material for histological examination: heart and other organs
n: We look at taking material for histological examination. In the standard set from the heart, the ventricular walls and the interventricular septum are taken together with endocardium and pericardium. In sudden death, material is taken from the anterior and posterior walls near the apex of the left ventricle, from the valve and the muscle, since infarction most often occurs there. When rheumatism and coronary thrombosis are suspected, it is expedient to take a piece with a coronary artery. Besides pieces of the heart, material from the brain, kidney, liver and lung is sent. Phase-contrast and polarising microscopy are used.

t: Case analysis 2: death of an adult man
n: Case analysis. Situation based on the source: an adult man died unexpectedly after heavy physical work. Atherosclerotic changes were found in the coronary vessels. Physical exertion may be the trigger and decompensate the disease. In adults, 85–90 per cent of unexpected death is cardiovascular. In ischaemia an arrhythmogenic substance is released from cardiomyocytes. After circulation is restored, it passes into the blood and may lead to ventricular fibrillation. Conclusion: if there is no clear infarct, acute coronary insufficiency and fibrillation are considered. First, signs of violent death are excluded.

Summary of the lesson. In sudden cardiac death, histology reveals contractures, fragmentation, microcirculatory changes and the stages of infarction. Myocarditis, fibrosis of the conduction system and uneven hypertrophy of cardiomyocytes are confirmed only by microscopic, and morphometric, examination. Coronary thrombosis is not the sole decisive evidence. In aortic rupture, signs of organisation indicate the age. If histological material is correctly taken, that is from the heart, brain, kidney, liver and lung, it is assessed together with the general morphological signs.
